## What "animal breeding" meant before DNA

In animal breeding, we select individuals with outstanding trait
performance to achieve better production outcomes and/or prevent
production loss, where historically breeders have relied on phenotypic
records. To achieve that, the standard evaluation tool, Best Linear
Unbiased Prediction (BLUP), combines records on the animal itself with
records on its relatives to produce an Estimated Breeding Value (EBV).
Essentially, a BLUP-EBV is just a regression on the animal's data and
pedigree that has already been produced, and it is updated as new
records come in and the pedigree grows.

Pedigree-based BLUP worked very well. It still works till now! National
dairy evaluation programmes, beef cattle indices, and pig and poultry
nucleus schemes all ran on phenotype + pedigree BLUP for decades, and
most of the genetic gain documented in production species before the
mid-2000s came out of exactly that loop.

However, the problem lies in gathering phenotypes and pedigree data. A
trait that is invasive, expensive, or late-expressed (e.g., disease
resistance, slaughter quality, longevity, fertility in young sires) is
hard to record in the selection candidates themselves. The traditional
solution was progeny testing, where we wait until the candidate has
daughters or sons with records, average their records, and call the
average the candidate's pseudo-phenotype. Progeny testing is accurate
but very slow! which is why generation intervals in dairy cattle stayed
long even after the BLUP machinery matured.

## The DNA promise

From 1990 onward, molecular genetics suggested an alternative with a
simple question. If genes underlying a trait could be located and
genotyped, that information could feed directly into BLUP-EBV without
waiting for the phenotype. So, Marker-Assisted Selection (MAS) comes
aboard with two-step procedures based on the Fernando and Grossman
(1989) framework:

1.  Detect and fine-map genes underlying the trait. These positions are
    called quantitative trait loci (QTL).
2.  Include the QTL information in the BLUP-EBV.

On the surface, both steps are defensible. The first is a statistical
search problem, while the second is a straightforward extension of the
linear mixed model. Yet in practice, the field hit two structural
problems that took fifteen years to diagnose properly.

## Why QTL mapping disappointed

Although many studies reported finding QTLs in specific genomic regions,
these studies have very low reproducibility and reliability. This is
because the position of QTLs can vary substantially between genotypes,
and segregation and recombination due to selection can also influence
the presence or absence of QTLs.

The mechanism is the Beavis effect (Beavis, 1994). When a large number
of markers are scanned for association with a trait, most of the true
effects are very small, while the few markers that happen to cross the
significance threshold are markers that have shifted upward by chance.
Therefore, the estimated effect is systematically overestimated and not
replicated in subsequent studies.

At a 1% significance level across 100 markers, one false positive is
expected even if every true effect is zero. Scaled to genome-wide
association studies with thousands of SNPs in livestock (and hundreds of
thousands in human genetics), the problem becomes severe enough to fail
to meet the $P < 5 \times 10^{-8}$ significance.

However, there are exceptions. A small number of QTLs with large effects
have been detected and used routinely. For example, DGAT1, which affects
milk fat content and CDH1, which affects resistance to infectious
pancreatic necrosis virus in Atlantic salmon. These are cases where a
single QTL captures enough variation to merit individual selection.
However, for most economically important traits, this does not hold
true.

The second problem is even more fundamental. In livestock, detected QTLs
account for less than 10% of genetic variance, despite extensive mapping
efforts. In 2005, for example, the application of MAS in production
breeding was extremely limited. Over 90% of genetic differences between
animals had to be addressed by traditional selection, making MAS a very
small substitute for phenotypic and pedigree frameworks.

## The missing-heritability paradox

A similar pattern emerges in human genetics. An extensive GWAS study,
for example, analysed genotypes from 160,000 individuals across 500,000
SNPs, but explained only a fraction of the total genetic variance for
the traits they targeted. This gap is called the missing heritability
paradox (Manolio et al., 2009).

However, there is at least one possible explanation: **the complex trait
is influenced by many genes with small effects**. Even when a large
number of individuals are genotyped, the individual effects are still
too small to pass statistical tests. Therefore, when aggregated, these
small-effect genes account for the vast majority of heritable variation.

The implications for animal breeding are quantitative. In 2001, Hayes
and Goddard (2001) estimated that 50 to 100 genes influence dairy cattle
traits, and even that estimate was considered high at the time. In 2016,
the same authors concluded that 2,000 to 10,000 genes per dairy cattle
trait were significant, representing an approximately 100-fold revision
in fifteen years.

Therefore, if a trait is regulated by thousands of genes with small
effects, MAS becomes irrelevant. Most genes will never pass the
significance threshold required to incorporate QTL information into
BLUP-EBV.

## A brief comparison between phenotypic BLUP and MAS

|   | Phenotypic + pedigree BLUP | Marker-Assisted Selection (MAS) |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Data** | Records on the animal and its relatives; pedigree | Phenotypic records + a small set of detected QTL genotypes |
| **EBV formula** | Linear function of phenotypic records weighted by the pedigree relationship matrix | BLUP-EBV with QTL effects added as fixed or random terms (Fernando & Grossman, 1989) |
| **Strengths** | Works without DNA; nationally implemented; well-understood theory | Uses DNA where it is informative; faster than waiting for progeny records |
| **Limits** | Slow for traits with late or invasive recording; requires deep pedigree | Limited by which QTL clear significance; Beavis effect inflates discovered effects; \<10% of breeding-objective variance captured by 2005 |

The next page is about the methodology that broke this ceiling: how the
field moved from "find a handful of large-effect QTL" to "estimate
effects on every marker in the panel at once".
